summary: This unit teaches you to keep the records a housekeeping department depends on: room status reports, worksheets, the logbook, lost and found, key control, maintenance requests, guest requests, linen counts and accident reports. You will learn to write accurate entries on paper and on a computer, find and deal with room status discrepancies, keep guest information confidential, file, archive and dispose of records correctly, and suggest improvements.

blocks.p: Housekeeping runs on information. Front office needs to know which rooms are clean and ready. The supervisor needs to know who cleaned what. A guest who lost a phone needs it found. A manager who has a missing key needs to know who held it. All of this depends on **records**: written or typed information that is accurate, complete and easy to find.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. A large hotel may use a property management system (PMS) with phone apps; a small villa may use a notebook and a spreadsheet. You need to be able to work with both.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks: completing housekeeping records for a busy shift from event cards, and setting up a filing system and an electronic lost and found log. The assessor looks for accuracy, neat writing, confidentiality and teamwork.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Housekeeping records and what they are for

head: Record
What it shows
Who uses it
rows: The state of each room: clean, dirty, occupied, vacant, out of order, Do Not Disturb
The rooms she must clean in the shift, with the status and special tasks
Messages, problems and unfinished jobs, passed on between shifts
Items found, where, when and by whom; and when claimed or returned
Who has each key, when it was issued and returned
A fault in a room or area and who must repair it
Extra items requested (pillows, iron, cot) and when delivered
Linen used, laundered, damaged and lost
Whether a room meets the standard
What happened when a person is hurt or something serious occurs

blocks.p: Records are kept to **track work, stock, keys and guest items**, to show that standards were met, to protect the property in a dispute, and to help the department plan. Months later, accident and lost property records may be needed for insurance, claims or the law.

Properties use **standard forms** so every worker records the same things in the same place. Use the current form, not your own notes. If a new attendant likes her own notebook, she must still use the property's form and system.

blocks.note: You are responsible for the accuracy of every entry you make. Write only facts: what you saw and did, not what you guess.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The exact codes differ between properties. Common ones are below: learn your property's list.

head: Status
Meaning
rows: Cleaned and inspected; ready for a guest
A guest is staying; clean or dirty
A guest is expected to check out today
A guest is staying another night
The guest has asked not to be disturbed
Cannot be sold because of a fault or repair

blocks.p: Update a room's status **as soon as it is finished** (on the phone app, the PMS or the paper report). Front office can then give the room to an arriving guest. Wrong or late status means a guest may be sent to a dirty room.

A **discrepancy** is a difference between the housekeeping room report and the front office list for the same room. Housekeeping sends its report to front office during the day, so that the two records can be compared.

head: Situation
Name and meaning
What to do
rows: Front office shows the room occupied, but the attendant finds no luggage and an unused bed
A **sleeper**: the room is empty but the front office record has not been updated
Recheck the room, tell the supervisor and front office so the record is corrected
A guest has left, with or without his luggage, without paying his bill
Do not touch belongings; tell the supervisor and front office; follow the property's rules
Housekeeping shows a room vacant, front office shows it occupied (or the other way round)
Recheck the room, record what you saw and report it; do not guess

blocks.note: Never assume which record is right. Recheck the room, record exactly what you saw, and tell the supervisor, who will speak to front office.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A DND sign on a door is respected. If it stays up for much of the day, note it on the room report. Many properties have a rule that the supervisor or front office checks on the guest's welfare (by phone or a knock) after a set time. Follow your property's rule.

Log every guest request (an extra pillow, an iron, a cot) with the room, the time requested, what was asked, who delivered it and the time. This makes sure each request is done and shows what was provided.

ul: The **date and time**.
The **room or place** and the **item or event**.
**Facts only**, in clear short words.
Your **name or initials and signature**.
Legible writing in ink (black or blue) for paper records.

blocks.p: Date, time and signature show **when** something happened and **who** wrote it.

flow: Draw one neat line through the mistake
Write the correct entry beside it
Write your initials and the date
Never use correction fluid or scribble out

blocks.p: The original must stay readable. That shows nothing is being hidden.

head: Poor
Better
rows: 14 Nov, 10:20. Room 214. Found black phone with cracked screen under bed. Found by A. Reid. Handed to Supervisor Brown.
14 Nov, 11:00. Room 305. Bathroom basin tap dripping constantly. Reported by M. Smith. Work order no. 118.
14 Nov, 15:30. Corridor, 2nd floor. Guest in room 208 raised his voice at attendant about late towels. Attendant stayed calm. Reported to Supervisor.

ul: Type in the correct field. Check spelling and numbers before you save.
Do not leave a field blank if it needs to be filled.
Save your work and log out when you finish.
A spreadsheet works best with **one column for each detail** (date, room, item, finder), so it can be sorted and searched.

blocks.p: The logbook passes jobs and messages from one shift to the next. Write the date and time, what happened or must be done, who is to do it, and sign. Read the logbook at the start of every shift. If something is unclear, ask.

sections.title: Lost and found, keys and maintenance

flow: Leave the item as found; do not search it more than needed
Note the place, date and time
Take it to the supervisor or security straight away
Write it in the lost and found register
Label the item with the number and store it in the lost property store
Return it only to the right owner and have it signed for

head: Register columns
Example
rows: Black phone, cracked screen, blue case

ul: Describe items by what you see: 'yellow metal ring', not 'gold ring'; 'clear stone', not 'diamond'. You cannot be sure of the value, and a wrong guess can cause trouble.
A caller says she left something: ask her to **describe it first** (colour, make, marks). Do not describe it for her.
Return an item only after the person has described it correctly and signed for it. Ask for ID if the rule says so.
Keep the items for the time the property's policy sets, then follow the rules for items nobody claims.

blocks.p: Keys, especially master keys, are among the most important items in housekeeping. A **key control log** records which key was issued, to whom, the date and time, and when it was returned, with signatures.

ul: Issue keys only to authorised staff and only for their shift.
Check keys back in at the end of the shift.
A key is missing: **report it at once** so that security and the manager can act (they may change the locks or check the doors).
Never lend a key, and never leave one in a door or on a trolley.

flow: Find the fault (a dripping tap, a broken lamp)
Complete a maintenance request or work order: room, fault, date, time, your name
Send it to maintenance and keep a copy or the number
Mark the room out of order if needed
Follow it up until it is fixed
Record the date it was completed and update the room status

blocks.note: A fault that is reported but not followed up is the guest's problem next day. Keep the work order number and check it every day until the job is done.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: If a guest or a worker is hurt (for example a guest slips in a corridor), fill in an **accident or incident report** as soon as possible. Write the date, time, place, what happened, who was involved, who saw it, what was done and who was told. Write facts only. These reports may be needed later for insurance, claims and the law.
Count linen daily or as the property says, and record what was sent to the laundry, returned, damaged and lost. This tracks use, laundering and loss, and it shows when to buy more.

A **property management system (PMS)** is the software a property uses to run the front desk, reservations and housekeeping. Housekeeping staff may use it on a computer, tablet or phone to see and update room status, and to log requests and faults. Other electronic records may be simple spreadsheets.

head: Point
Paper (manual) records
Electronic records
rows: Works without power or the internet
Easy for any staff to read
Easy to copy and back up
Can be lost, damaged or hard to read
One copy: others cannot see it at once
Needs power, the internet and training
Can be lost if not backed up
Can be seen by the wrong people if passwords are shared

ul: Use **your own** login and password. Never share it, write it on the desk or let anyone else use it.
If a co-worker's password is not working, she must ask the supervisor, not borrow yours.
**Lock the screen or log off** when you step away, even for a minute.
Only open files you need for your job.

blocks.p: A **backup** is a copy of computer records kept in case the original is lost. Records are backed up regularly (daily or weekly) to a second place (a different drive or a secure cloud service). Backups are protected like the originals, because they hold the same information.

ul: Put the headings in the first row (Date, Room, Item, Found by).
One record per row, one detail per column.
Sort by date or by room to find records quickly.
Save often and save a copy with the date in the file name.
Do not mix words and numbers in one cell.

blocks.note: If the PMS is down, use paper forms and enter them into the system as soon as it is working. Do not lose information.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Guest and staff records hold names, room numbers, phone numbers, passports, card details, health details and addresses. This is **personal information**. The law and the property's rules protect it, and Jamaica has a data protection law whose purpose is to protect people's personal information. Guests trust the property to keep it private.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: A visitor asks you who is staying in Room 112
Refuse politely; send him to the front desk. Do not read from your worksheet.
A caller asks if a famous person is staying
Say you cannot give out guest information
A guest's file is open on a computer you leave
Lock the screen or log off
Keep them in a locked cabinet in the office; never leave them on a counter or trolley
Records you no longer need to keep
Shred them as the rules say; do not put them in the bin
A co-worker asks about a guest 'for fun'
Do not share: information is shared only on a need-to-know basis

ul: Do not discuss guests where others can hear.
Do not photograph records, or take them home.
Keep your worksheet with you, or in a safe place.
Staff records are private too: pay, discipline and health details.

blocks.note: Never read out a room number with a guest's name in a public area. If you must tell a guest which room to go to, say the number quietly and in private.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Method
How it works
Used for
rows: A to Z, usually by surname
Guest history cards, staff files, supplier files
Room numbers, work orders, forms with serial numbers
In date order, newest or oldest first
Daily reports, lost and found forms, linen counts, rotas
By topic (for example Maintenance, Uniforms, Policies)

blocks.p: Choose the method that makes records easiest to find. Many properties use more than one: for example, folders by month (chronological) with guest cards inside in A to Z order.

blocks.h: Keeping a filing system in order

ul: Label every folder, drawer and shelf clearly.
Keep an **index sheet** that lists what is where.
Put a file back in its place straight after use, so others can find it fast.
Use an 'out' card when you take a file away.
Do not overfill folders; start a new one.
Keep files in a clean, dry place, safe from damp, pests and fire.

blocks.p: Records are not kept for ever. Each type has a **keeping period** set by the property, and some by law. Old records are not thrown away at once.

flow: Check the keeping period
Move records past active use to the archive
Keep them safe for the set time
Check that nobody needs them
Destroy them, shredding anything with personal details
Record what was destroyed and when

head: Word
What it means
rows: A safe store for old records kept for a set time
Cutting papers into small pieces so they cannot be read
How long a record must be kept

blocks.note: Never put paper with guest names, card numbers or phone numbers in an ordinary bin. Shred it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A records system only works if **everyone** uses it. If one attendant keeps her own notebook while others use the PMS, information is lost and mistakes follow.

ul: Use the property's **current forms and systems**, not your own.
Record events at the time or as soon as possible, not at the end of the week.
Check that your records match those of other departments, for example by comparing your room report with front office's list.
Hand over your records and messages at the change of shift.
Ask for training if you do not understand a form or a screen.

blocks.p: If a form never asks for something important (for example, the time a request was done), or an entry takes too long, do not change it yourself. Tell your supervisor politely, explain the problem, and suggest a better way. A good idea may be added to the form.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Report mistakes in the records you find
Tell the supervisor if a form is out of date
Keep using an old form quietly

ul: I can name the main housekeeping records and say what each is used for.
I can explain why records must be accurate, dated, timed and signed.
I can write a clear entry and correct a mistake with one line and my initials.
I can explain room status words and why status must be updated at once.
I can explain a discrepancy, a sleeper and a skipper, and say what housekeeping and front office do about them.
I can record a found item without guessing its value and check a claim by asking the caller to describe it first.
I can use a key control log and say what to do when a key is missing.
I can complete a maintenance request and follow it up until it is done.
I can say when an accident or incident report is needed and what it contains.
I can use a PMS and spreadsheet safely: my own password, lock the screen, save and back up.
I can compare paper and electronic systems.
I can keep guest and staff information confidential on paper and on computers.
I can file by alphabetical, numerical and chronological order and say when each is best.
I can say what an archive is and how old records are destroyed.
I can say why I must use the current forms and how to suggest an improvement.

terms: Written or electronic information kept as proof of what happened.
Property management system: the software used to run reservations, front desk and housekeeping.
The record of the state of each room.
The list of rooms an attendant must clean in a shift.
The shared book for messages and unfinished jobs between shifts.
A difference between two records of the same thing.
A room that front office shows as occupied but is found empty and unused.
A guest who leaves without paying the bill.
The record of items found and returned.
The record of who holds each key.
A request for maintenance to repair a fault.
A copy of computer records kept in case the original is lost.
A safe store for old records.
Cutting papers into small pieces so they cannot be read.

c1.title: Room 110 at a small hotel in Treasure Beach
c1.text: At a small hotel in Treasure Beach, room attendant Alicia receives her worksheet. Front office shows Room 110 as occupied, but when she enters at 9:30 a.m. the bed has not been slept in, the bathroom is dry and there is no luggage. In Room 114 a guest checked out an hour ago and the room is now cleaned and inspected. The phone app still shows it as dirty.

c2.title: Lost items at a Falmouth hotel
c2.text: At a hotel in Falmouth, attendant Devon finds a silver tablet in a black case and a pair of gold-coloured earrings in a checked-out room. Later the same day a woman phones and says she left her tablet in Room 207. The front desk clerk asks housekeeping to confirm. The lost and found register is kept in the housekeeping office.

c3.title: The housekeeping computer in Kingston
c3.text: At a business hotel in Kingston, supervisor Mrs. Campbell leaves the housekeeping computer open on the room status screen while she checks a corridor. A co-worker, Rohan, says his login is locked and asks to use the attendant's password, which she has written on a card taped to the desk. Later a man at the counter says he is a friend of a guest and asks which room the guest is in.

c4.title: Filing at a guest house in Savanna-la-Mar
c4.text: A guest house in Savanna-la-Mar has a box of mixed records: guest history cards, maintenance work orders numbered 201 to 240, daily linen counts for the month, a pile of papers on the house policies for uniforms, safety and training, and a stack of old guest registration forms from six years ago. The owner wants everything filed so that any record can be found in under two minutes, and the old forms dealt with correctly.

c5.title: Keys and a fall at a Port Maria villa
c5.text: At a villa in Port Maria, attendant Natalie signs out a master key at 8:00 a.m. At 4:00 p.m. she cannot find it and realises it may have fallen from her pocket. During the day a guest slipped on the wet tiles of the corridor and bruised her arm, and the attendant also found a leaking pipe in the pantry. The villa uses a key log, a maintenance request form and an accident report form.

questions.q: What is the situation in Room 110 called?
o: A sleeper: empty room, shown as occupied
A skipper, because the guest left without paying
A late check-out, because the room is still occupied
A stay-over, because the guest stays another night
questions.why: A room that front office shows as occupied, but where the housekeeper finds no luggage and an unused bed, is a sleeper. The records need checking and correcting.

questions.q: What should Alicia do about Room 110?
o: Clean it and then mark it as vacant ready herself
Leave it and carry on with the next room
Ask the guest's neighbour if he is in
Recheck it and tell her supervisor what she saw
questions.why: She must not guess which record is right. She rechecks the room, records what she saw and tells the supervisor, who will speak to front office.

questions.q: Alicia has finished and inspected Room 114. When should she update its status?
o: At the end of her shift, with the other rooms
After lunch, when the app is quiet
As soon as the room is finished
When the next guest arrives at the desk
questions.why: Front office can only give the room to an arriving guest when its status is correct. Late updates send guests to dirty rooms or leave clean rooms unused.

questions.q: Why does housekeeping send its room report to the front office during the day?
o: So that front office can clean rooms for housekeeping
So that the two records can be compared for differences
So that guests can see which rooms are ready
So that housekeeping can change front office's bookings
questions.why: Comparing the two lists shows discrepancies early, such as sleepers, skippers and rooms with the wrong status, so they can be fixed before guests are affected.

questions.q: How should Devon describe the earrings in the lost and found register?
o: Gold-coloured earrings, as the metal is not certain
Gold earrings, worth a lot of money
Expensive earrings left by a wealthy guest
Earrings, value to be decided later by the supervisor
questions.why: Staff describe what they see and do not guess the material or value. A wrong guess can cause a dispute if the item is claimed.

questions.q: What should happen first when the woman phones about her tablet?
o: Devon tells her the tablet is in a black case
The clerk posts it to her at once without questions
The clerk tells her it is in Room 207 under the bed
She describes it and the clerk checks the register
questions.why: Asking the caller to describe the item first shows whether she really owns it. Staff must not give details that would let someone else make a false claim.

questions.q: What must be recorded when the tablet is given back to its owner?
o: Only that the tablet is no longer in the cupboard
The owner's phone number and her room rate
The date, who got it and her signature
Nothing, as the item has now gone
questions.why: The register must show the item was returned, to whom, when, and a signature proves it. This protects the owner and the property.

questions.q: Where should the tablet and earrings be kept until they are claimed?
o: In the housekeeping office, on the desk
In the lost property store, with a label
In the attendant's locker, for safety
On the trolley, so she can show them to guests
questions.why: Found items are stored securely and labelled with their register number, so they can be found and are not lost or taken.

questions.q: What should Mrs. Campbell have done before she left the computer?
o: Locked the screen or logged off
Minimised the page and left it
Turned the monitor away from the desk
Asked Rohan to watch the screen
questions.why: An open screen lets anyone read or change records using her login. Lock it or log off every time you step away, however briefly.

questions.q: Rohan asks to use another attendant's password. What is the correct reply?
o: Agree, but only for a few minutes
Agree, if he promises not to change anything
Refuse, but tell him how to find the password on the card
Refuse; he should ask the supervisor to fix his login
questions.why: Passwords are personal. If a colleague uses yours, the records show your name, and you are responsible for what is done. The supervisor can reset his login.

questions.q: What is wrong with a password written on a card taped to the desk?
o: The password is too long to fit on a card
The card may fade, so she forgets the password
Anyone passing can read it and log in as her
It breaks the rule on changing passwords weekly
questions.why: A password written where others can see it is no longer secret. Memorise it, and if it must be recorded, keep it somewhere private.

questions.q: What should the attendant say to the man who asks which room his 'friend' is in?
o: Look at the worksheet and tell him the room number
Politely refuse and refer him to the front desk
Tell him the floor but not the room number
Say it is best to ask the guest's neighbour
questions.why: Guest details are private. Even a floor number can put a guest at risk. The front desk can contact the guest and let him decide.

questions.q: The owner also has papers on the guest house policies for uniforms, safety and training. Which filing method suits them best?
o: By subject, with a label for each topic
By the date they were printed, oldest first
By the surname of the person who wrote them
In number order, using the page numbers
questions.why: Policy papers are looked for by topic, so filing by subject with clear labels is quickest. Alphabetical suits names, numerical suits numbered forms and chronological suits dated records.

questions.q: The work orders are numbered 201 to 240. Which filing method suits them best?
o: Alphabetical order
Order of date of the fault
By the colour of the form
Numerical order
questions.why: Numbered documents are easiest to find when kept in number order, so a missing number can be spotted at once.

questions.q: The guest registration forms are six years old. What should the owner do first?
o: Put them in the bin with all the ordinary rubbish
Keep them in the front desk drawer for ever
Check the keeping period, then archive or shred
Give them back to the guests who signed them
questions.why: Old records are kept for the period set by the property and the law. After that, forms with personal details are shredded, not thrown away whole.

questions.q: Why does the owner keep an index sheet in the filing cabinet?
o: So that only the owner can find the records
So anyone can find a record quickly
So that the cabinet can be left unlocked
So that old records can be thrown away sooner
questions.why: An index lists what is filed where. A system that only one person understands is slow and puts records at risk when she is absent.

questions.q: What should Natalie do first when she cannot find the master key?
o: Report it at once to her supervisor and security
Search the whole villa before telling anyone
Wait until the end of her shift to see if it appears
Borrow another attendant's key and say nothing
questions.why: A missing master key is a security risk to every room. Reporting it quickly lets the supervisor and manager decide whether to check doors or change locks.

questions.q: What should be written in the key log about the lost key?
o: Only that the key was lost, with no details
Nothing, because the key is no longer in use
That the key was stolen, to be on the safe side
Time missed, last place seen, who was told
questions.why: The log should state facts: when it was missed, where it was last seen and who was informed. Never write a guess, such as theft, as fact.

questions.q: Which details belong in the accident report about the guest who slipped?
o: Who Natalie thinks was to blame and how to punish them
Only the injured guest's name and room number
Date, time, place, what happened and who saw it
The guest's account, written up the following week
questions.why: An accident report states facts: when, where, what happened, who saw it, what was done and who was told. Opinions about blame are left out, and the report is written as soon as possible.

questions.q: Natalie reports the leaking pipe using a maintenance request. What should she do next?
o: Forget it, since maintenance will see the leak
Keep the number and check each day until fixed
Mop the area every day and drop the request
Ask the guest to follow it up with maintenance
questions.why: A reported fault must be followed up until it is repaired. The request number lets her check progress and update the room or area status when the job is done.
